newsitem.title: UK: World oil prices as volatile as the weather.
newsitem.headline: World oil prices as volatile as the weather.

text.p: World oil prices reversed early losses in extremely volatile trade on Thursday, in a market held to ransom by the weather, oil traders said.
London February futures for benchmark North Sea Brent blend closed six cents higher at $23.96 per barrel, having recovered from a low of $23.62.
With oil stocks running at historical lows in key western markets, prices have become ultra-sensitive to the vagaries of the elements.
"The market is fundamentally well-supported, but it can jump either way on perceptions of the weather," said Charles Gray of Prudential Bache futures brokers in London.

Bone-chilling temperatures have swept the United States this week, and forecasters are predicting more of the same with a cold front expected to hit the Midwest by early next week, pulling temperatures about 10 degrees below normal.
But all eyes were on the U.S. Gulf coast refining belt in Texas and Louisiana, where refineries will have to cope with the demand surge from sub-zero temperatures which could send prices soaring.
"Because stocks are so low there's no cushion to deal with production problems or any other disruptions," an oil trader said.

As Christmas approaches and trade thins, analysts said that diminishing trading volumes are adding to the market's instability. "A lot of people are easing out of the market so it's becoming thinner and potentially more volatile," said Gray.
Against this backdrop, analysts said the world market would have little difficulty in absorbing Iraqi crude exports under the United Nations oil-for-food agreement.

Iraq said on Thursday it had signed oil export contracts with 23 companies. It is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of crude oil over six months to buy humanitarian supplies, the first international sales since the U.N. put up sanctions after Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Ship brokers said two tankers of Iraqi crude have already loaded at the Middle East Gulf terminal of Mina al-Bakr destined for the U.S. and the Caribbean.

And in the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan, Turkey's state oil company Tupras bought the first cargo of Iraqi crude to be sent down the Iraq-Turkey pipeline, and three more vessels with European destinations were scheduled to load there before the end of the year.
